program: Violence intervention, trauma support, education and employment

what: Chicago CRED works with people at high risk of gun violence on Chicago's South and West sides.
Its outreach, therapy and life coaching are paired with education and employment support.
It also funds local partners and helps coordinate the city's violence-intervention ecosystem.
strengths: Long-term relationships can connect high-risk participants with sustained support.
Paid internships and employer partnerships offer a practical route into legal employment.
Direct services and grants address both individual barriers and neighborhood capacity.
reservations: Observational arrest reductions do not establish injuries prevented.
Citywide and ecosystem results cannot be assigned entirely to CRED or a new gift.
Net earnings, attendance burdens and the response to additional donations remain unmeasured.

sections.what: Chicago CRED Inc, EIN 81-3130448, is the legal recipient. Its official site now links a current Give Lively donation page, replacing the closed historical Network for Good campaign. The linked page was accessible, but no transaction or fulfillment was verified. South and West Side service delivery establishes Chicago beneficiaries despite the tax filing's California address. [Current services](https://www.chicagocred.org/)
sections.monitoring: CRED offers outreach, trauma therapy, life coaching, education, paid internships and employment support, with a year of coaching after job placement. Its 2025 report describes direct services, partner grants and SC2 coordination. Historical grants exceeding $50 million since 2016 and ecosystem estimates of 383 shootings prevented are cumulative or multi-organization results, not annual CRED causal outcomes. Track distinct participants, completion, victimization, validated trauma symptoms, collected disposable earnings and alternatives. Public sector funding for partner programs remains in the baseline.
sections.qualitative: Northwestern compared 324 recruited men with a balanced comparison group of 2,500. The evaluation was observational, not randomized. Program completers had substantially fewer violent-crime arrests, but firearms victimization remained statistically unchanged. Completer selection, changing neighborhood conditions and policing can affect apparent results. Arrests are not physical QALYs, and the 73% arrest result is not an intent-to-treat injury coefficient. The injury and trauma values below are conditional weak planning priors, not translated study estimates. The unknown and clinical-null cases preserve this distinction.
sections.cost:
Calendar 2024 original Form 990-PF reports $36,314,414 total book expenses. Its $37,047,914 charitable cash disbursements are a different accounting measure, not an addback. The whole recognized annual recipient cost includes direct work, grants, administration and other activities; it is not a restricted participant-program denominator. No equivalent Form 990 netted event/rental addback was identified. Outside implementation and social costs remain separate.

A judged 400 local household opportunities and .5 annual-package response imply 200 exposed households, with 100 clinical participants. A .05 annual victimization risk and .05 causal reduction imply .25 avoided physical victimizations. One integrated injury QALY per event is truncated within three years and excludes trauma. The remaining 99.75 people receive .03 trauma utility for half a year. Positive clinical components retain .8 for overlap; harms remain full. A one-year delay and 3% discount produce 1.356311 clinical QALYs.

The clinical cohort is a subset of the 200 resource-exposed households; one participant household carries one modeled welfareperson, with other family welfare unpriced. Resource exposure remains when clinical benefit fails. Fifty households have judged net job resources of $1,500 and net stipends of $300. Positive components each retain .5, then full attendance costs of $300 are subtracted: $600 net. The other 150 households net −$150. Negative components are never attenuated by overlap. A single joint household log gives .5 × [50 log(1.04) + 150 log(.99)] / 1.03 = .220138 equivalent healthy years at a $15,000 household baseline for one finite year. Combined 1.576449 yields $230.355757 million per ten combined equivalents, not ten clinical QALYs.

Job gains are after taxes, benefit withdrawal, replacement earnings and new-job commuting or care costs; stipends are after taxes and benefits. Class attendance, early foregone work and travel are separate full burdens. These amounts are hypotheses, not observed gains. No ordinary survivor wages are added. Central payer and external care incidence is unknown-neutral, not factual zero. Matched stipend-payer losses, external costs, negative resource changes, adverse trauma and mixed-sign cases are explicit. Household gains and losses combine before one log; distinct payer households are modeled separately. Whole portfolio and nonlocal incidence remain unknown.
sections.funding: Comparable calendar 2022, 2023 and 2024 book expenses are $34,196,858, $33,370,210 and $36,314,414, mean $34,627,160.67. Contributions in 2024 are $26,010,890 and net assets $16,146,226. The current impact report describes CRED as privately funded while partners increasingly receive public support. This is not evidence that an additional gift expands services rather than replacing another donor. The .5 response prior judges additional annual funded work against alternatives; b=1 shows full response. No specific marginal expansion cost was verified. Existing coalition appropriations and historical projects are not credited anew. [Original return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202522209349101107/IRS990PF)

model.geographicAttribution: Chicago South and West Side household cohort; clinical participants are a subset of resource exposure.
model.formula: events=N*b*uptake*risk*reduction; clinical=positiveOnly(events*injuryQ,k)+positiveOnly((treated-events)*traumaQ*traumaYears,k), minus full harms, discounted once. Resources=.5*people*log(1+joint net household change/baseline), one year after one-year delay. Price=10*annual book cost/(clinical+resources).
model.counterfactual: Existing public violence prevention, employment and trauma services continue; alternative jobs, benefit offsets and funding replacement matter.
model.attribution: All population, risk, uptake, response, efficacy and resource success coefficients are conditional judgments, not recipient causal observations.
model.uncertainty: Conditional reference with unknown complete portfolio and marginal-gift effects; observational arrest findings do not identify injury or resource priors.
model.nativeOutcomes: Finite physical injury and trauma improvements, collected net household job and stipend resources, full attendance burdens and counterparty losses.
